title: How to overcome the productivity pains of digital transformation? The U‑shaped TFP trajectory of Chinese agricultural firms, fixed‑asset constraints and subsidy threshold effects
summary: Digital transformation has profoundly reshaped agricultural production systems, yet its productivity effects remain insufficiently explored. Using panel data of Chinese listed agricultural firms from 2010 to 2022, this paper examines the effects, mechanisms, moderation, and heterogeneity of digital transformation on total factor productivity (TFP). First, digital transformation exerts a significant U-shaped nonlinear effect on TFP: the linear coefficient is −0.154 ( p < 0.01), and the squared coefficient is 0.036 ( p < 0.01), indicating that early-stage fixed asset accumulation, organizational restructuring, and system adaptation frictions drag down TFP, while after crossing the critical threshold, network synergy and factor allocation optimization drive sustained TFP growth. Second, the fixed asset-to-revenue ratio serves as a key transmission channel, forming a nonlinear mediation path of “digitalization → fixed asset-to-sales ratio → TFP.” Bootstrap tests show that the indirect effect turns from negative to positive as digitalization increases and is significant only at high levels. Third, government subsidies significantly moderate the U-shaped relationship, shifting the turning point leftward and increasing curvature, reflecting a “turning point forward shift and dividend amplification” mechanism. Fourth, the U-shaped relationship is more pronounced for non-state-owned, small-scale, and livestock enterprises. Theoretically, this paper constructs a nonlinear mediation framework of “digitalization–asset structure–TFP,” reveals the inverted U-shaped transmission of the fixed asset-to-revenue ratio, identifies the nonlinear moderating role of government subsidies, and enriches research on digital transformation and agricultural TFP. Practically, it suggests establishing a “pain period” tolerance mechanism, shifting subsidies toward soft support, and precisely supporting non-state-owned, small-scale, and livestock enterprises to release productivity dividends.

title: Consumer Preference Analysis of Financial Technology Application Services in a Developing Economy: A Maximum Difference Scaling Approach
summary: ABSTRACT Situated in a developing economy context, this study explores what matters most to users when they engage with financial technology (Fintech) applications. Rather than assuming a uniform set of needs, we used Maximum Difference (MaxDiff) scaling and Random Utility Theory (RUT) to unpack how people rank nine attributes including security, ease of use, service charges, and platform type. The results show that users place the greatest emphasis on security, affordability, and usability, while attributes like regulatory backing and years of operation matter less. Interestingly, these preferences vary across demographic groups, such as age, gender, and education. The findings offer practical insight into how fintech service providers can tailor their platforms to support better‐informed consumer decisions, particularly by improving simplicity, safety, and cost fairness. The application of RUT and MaxDiff provides a robust and scalable framework for understanding user priorities, providing a basis for replication in other Fintech contexts.

title: A bibliometric review of the gender diversity and ESG nexus in sustainability transformation
summary: The current study describes the scientific discourse around the interrelatedness of board gender diversity, environmental, social and governance (ESG) outcomes and corporate sustainability. It distinguishes ESG performance from ESG disclosure and explores the connections between those variables and sustainability transformation. The literature review covers 142 scientific papers, indexed in Scopus, published during 2016–2025. In addition to conventional narrative content analysis, this review utilizes bibliometric analysis, bibliographic coupling and keyword co-occurrence analysis. Document-level bibliographic coupling yielded six clusters among 128 interrelated documents, 14 documents being disconnected from the connected component. In a different set of analysis, an examination of 51 retained keywords yielded five clusters. The mapped literature covers topics of ESG performance and disclosure, governance and board oversight, legitimacy of stakeholders, sustainability and financial outcomes and institutional context. The reviewed studies frequently report positive associations between board gender diversity and ESG-related outcomes, although findings vary with outcome measurement, institutional setting, industry and research design. The study contributes through an integrated research map, clearer distinctions among sustainability-related constructs, and a cluster-linked research agenda.

title: Saudi Arabian and Emirati Climate Diplomacy toward Pacific Island Countries: Motivations, Practices, and Limits
summary: Why do hydrocarbon-exporting states pursue climate diplomacy toward Pacific Island countries that call for an accelerated fossil-fuel transition? This article compares Saudi Arabian and Emirati engagement from 2010 to September 2026 through a qualitative analysis of official documents, regional communiques, climate-policy texts, project records, and scholarly literature. It combines status seeking, niche diplomacy, institutional assets, and recipient agency in a framework linking motivations, practices, and outcomes. The findings show that economic diversification, reputational pressures, and wider South-South engagement motivate both states, but their institutional resources generate different diplomatic pathways. The United Arab Emirates follows a project-technology-institution model based on renewable-energy delivery, specialized agencies, and multilateral platforms. Saudi Arabia follows a finance-forum-politics model centered on major pledges, ministerial convening, and high-level diplomatic outreach. Pacific Island countries filter both approaches through regional priorities, partnership rules, and fossil-fuel-free norms. Consequently, Gulf engagement has produced tangible functional benefits and some institutional access, but limited normative convergence. The article argues that climate finance becomes diplomatic influence only when commitments are implemented, embedded in Pacific-led institutions, and judged consistent with recipient-defined climate priorities. It thereby explains both the possibilities and the structural limits of hydrocarbon exporters' climate diplomacy in highly climate-vulnerable regions.

title: Evaluating Financial Management Practices in the Department of Social Welfare and Development Field Office VII (DSWD FO VII): Proposed Process Integration Scheme
summary: Effective financial management is essential for the operational efficiency and accountability of public sector organizations. This study assessed the financial management practices of the Department of Social Welfare and Development Field Office VII (DSWD FO VII), focusing on record-keeping methods, financial reporting procedures, internal control measures, and document management practices. It also evaluated the effectiveness of these practices in relation to the Department’s Key Result Areas (KRAs), including fiscal policy formulation, fiscal management, technical assistance on financial concerns, and financial reporting and documentation. Furthermore, the study identified technical, organizational, financial, and operational issues encountered by the Financial Management Division (FMD). A descriptive survey design was employed, with purposive sampling of sixty-five (65) respondents from the Accounting, Budget, and Cash Sections of DSWD FO VII. Data were gathered through a researcher-made questionnaire and analyzed using frequency and percentage, ranking, weighted mean, chi-square test of independence, and scoring procedures. Findings revealed that financial management practices are generally highly practiced, particularly in financial reporting and fiscal management, while technical assistance and document management practices indicated moderate adherence. Key challenges identified include limited technical training, insufficient staffing, delays in budget releases, and operational inefficiencies. Statistical analysis also demonstrated a significant relationship between the level of financial management practices and their effectiveness in achieving the Department’s KRAs. Based on these findings, a process integration scheme was proposed to enhance operational efficiency, ensure effective resource utilization, and strengthen accountability within DSWD FO VII. This study underscores the importance of systematic financial management practices as critical drivers for achieving organizational objectives and promoting transparency in public service delivery.

title: Leading Through Cash Flow Volatility: How CEO Integrity Mitigates Insolvency Risk
summary: Abstract This research examines the relationship between cash flow volatility and insolvency risk, with a specific focus on the moderating effect of CEO integrity among Pakistani non-financial corporations. By incorporating the concept of ethical leadership into the finance risk management literature, this research makes a significant contribution to the body of corporate governance research on emerging markets. Using the Generalised Method of Moments (GMM) with dynamic panel data, the empirical analysis uses a dataset of 103 listed non-financial firms on the Pakistan Stock Exchange (PSX) from 2012 to 2019. The findings provide evidence of a significant positive relationship between cash flow volatility and the risk of insolvency. Our results suggest that CEOs who demonstrate high integrity exhibit a reduced impact of cash flow volatility on the risk of insolvency. The findings are pertinent to the understanding of governance processes that can be used to reinforce organizational stability during financial uncertainty, especially within the context of Pakistan’s emerging corporate environment.

title: Identity verification in virtual shareholders’ meetings: normative foundations and legal consequences
summary: Abstract The digital transformation of corporate governance has rendered virtual shareholders’ meetings a permanent feature of modern company law. While electronic participation enhances accessibility and cross-border engagement, it raises fundamental questions concerning the reliable identification of participants. This article examines identity verification in virtual shareholders’ meetings of private limited companies under Estonian law, with comparative references to German law. The analysis is based on the understanding that identity verification is not a mere technical formality but constitutes a structural precondition for the lawful formation of the company’s collective will. Although Estonian law permits electronic participation by default, it does not prescribe any specific authentication standards. The legal requirement that only shareholders or duly authorised representatives may exercise membership rights therefore remains unchanged, while the technical means used to ensure compliance vary. The article adopts a functional perspective on identity verification. It examines different forms of authentication that may be used in virtual meetings, including the Estonian state e-identity, other digital identification means (such as those recognised under the eIDAS framework), as well as situations where no formal digital identification is available. The discussion highlights how varying degrees of technical reliability may influence legal certainty and the protection of participation rights. Particular attention is given to the legal consequences of defective identification. Drawing on Estonian case law concerning digital signatures, the article analyses the presumption arising from the use of electronic identification tools, the formal requirements of representation, and the distinction between void votes and the revocation or nullity of resolutions. It argues that identity verification serves a procedural legitimising function and does not replace the substantive determination of share ownership. Virtual meetings therefore require not the creation of new legal principles but a careful functional adaptation of established company-law concepts to a technologically mediated environment.

title: Geopolitical Risk and Equity Markets: Supply-Chain Exposure and Stock-Market Reactions to the 2019 US–China Tariffs
summary: Abstract Geopolitical developments, including trade restrictions and tariffs, can disrupt international supply chains and influence financial markets. However, companies may experience different stock-market reactions depending on their exposure to affected countries and suppliers. This study investigates the extent to which supply-chain exposure predicts stock-market reactions among publicly listed textile and apparel companies following the 2019 increase in United States tariffs on Chinese imports. Historical share-price data, market-index returns, and corporate disclosures will be collected to measure companies' financial performance and dependence on affected supply chains. An event-study methodology will be used to calculate abnormal returns and cumulative abnormal returns (CAR) around the selected event. A cross-sectional regression will then examine the relationship between supply-chain exposure and CAR, controlling for relevant company characteristics where data permit. The study aims to assess whether differences in supply-chain exposure help explain variations in stock-market reactions to geopolitical trade actions. Its findings may contribute to understanding how international supply-chain structures influence firms' financial vulnerability. However, the analysis will recognise limitations arising from incomplete corporate disclosures, anticipated policy changes, and other market developments occurring around the event.

title: Technologically driven corporate sustainability: hospitality and tourism and fintech
summary: Purpose This article aims to reveal the impact, mechanism of action and boundary conditions (heterogeneity) of fintech on the environmental, social and governance (ESG) performance of listed hotel and tourism enterprises in China, thereby constructing a theoretical framework for understanding the relationship between the two and enriching and expanding the theory of sustainable development of enterprises. Design/methodology/approach We select 148 Chinese-listed hospitality and tourism as the research sample, empirically examine the role of fintech on the ESG performance of these firms and explore their potential influence mechanisms. Findings This study finds that fintech significantly enhances firm ESG performance. Moreover, fintech improves ESG performance of firms through financing constraints and external monitoring, while business risk mitigates the positive effects of fintech on firm ESG performance. The heterogeneity analysis indicates that the positive effect of fintech is more pronounced for regions with lower economic policy uncertainty and lower environmental regulation, as well as firms with high digitization and nonstate ownership. Research limitations/implications Firstly, there are deficiencies in the measurement of fintech. Future research will employ big data, text mining and machine learning technologies to develop more accurate fintech measurement indicators and mitigate endogenous issues such as measurement errors. Secondly, this article delves into the purview of fintech in influencing the H.T. firms' ESG performance from financing constraints, external supervision and business risks. Future research will utilize multidisciplinary cross-fertilization methods to further explore how fintech influences ESG performance. Thirdly, the current ESG disclosure of Chinese-listed firms is voluntary, and the conclusions drawn from this may have some limitations. Originality/value With the rapid advancement of fintech, H.T. firms have increasingly recognized its importance in addressing challenges related to difficult and costly financing. Nonetheless, the existing literature reveals substantial gaps in understanding how fintech influences H.T. firms' ESG performance, particularly due to the absence of a unified framework for systematically examining underlying mechanisms and boundary conditions. Accordingly, this study seeks to develop a multi-level explanatory framework that integrates information asymmetry theory, financing constraint theory, reputation theory and resource dependence theory. This framework enables a more comprehensive understanding of the transmission mechanisms and boundary conditions through which fintech influences ESG performance in H.T. firms, while providing a rational explanation of how fintech can optimize investment decision-making within these enterprises.

title: Firm’s financial flexibility, corporate governance, and investment efficiency: The evidence from an emerging country
summary: Using data from Vietnamese non-financial listed companies between 2010 and 2024, this study investigates the determinants of investment efficiency, specifically focusing on the dual problems of overinvestment and underinvestment. To achieve these research objectives, the study employs the System Generalised Method of Moments (SGMM) estimation technique to analyse the data and obtain robust empirical results. First, our empirical findings reveal that higher financial flexibility provides firms with readily available internal funds. However, these abundant financial resources tend to weaken external monitoring and increase managerial discretion, thereby fostering overinvestment. Similarly, state ownership exhibits a positive and significant relationship with investment inefficiency. This aligns with the soft-budget-constraints theory, where anticipated state backing dilutes financial discipline and drives overinvestment. Conversely, firm size is negatively correlated with investment inefficiency, indicating that the superior monitoring and governance inherent in larger firms effectively restrain managerial discretion. At the macro level, economic booms and loosened lending standards further amplify free cash flow problems and soften firms’ budget constraints, thereby exacerbating investment inefficiency. Ultimately, the findings of this study provide policymakers and managers with actionable recommendations to strengthen the Vietnamese corporate finance landscape and promote greater investment efficiency.

title: Environmental, Social, and Governance Performance as a Driver of Green Innovation: Evidence from Green Patent Data
summary: ABSTRACT This study examines the relationship between environmental, social, and governance (ESG) performance and firms' green innovation (GI), positioning ESG as an organizational context potentially conducive to sustainable technological transformation. Using a patent‐based methodology, GI is measured through firms' granted green patent outputs, providing a tangible indicator of green technological innovation. Based on 3314 firm‐year observations from 17 countries over 2002–2021, baseline estimations use OLS models with multiple fixed effects, complemented by count‐data and alternative specifications. The findings show a positive and statistically significant relationship between ESG performance and GI, which remains consistent across alternative specifications. The environmental, social, and governance dimensions are each positively associated with green patent output, with the environmental dimension exhibiting the largest coefficient in the baseline estimates. Additional mechanism analyses indicate that R&D intensity and analyst coverage serve as significant partial mediating channels. R&D intensity represents a firm‐internal innovation input, whereas analyst coverage captures external information and monitoring environment. Overall, the findings provide cross‐country evidence that ESG performance is associated with tangible green technological outcomes and suggest that this relationship may operate through both internal resource allocation and external information and monitoring channels.

title: Constructing the Mekong Intermediary Space: A Discourse Analysis of Strategic Narratives and the “Hinge State” in Vietnam–Thailand Relations
summary: Vietnam–Thailand’s elevation to a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership in May 2025 marks a critical juncture in mainland Southeast Asian diplomacy. Although this relationship is formally bilateral, the two countries describe their cooperation as connecting supply chains, local economies, and sustainable development strategies through “Mekong-centered sub-regional cooperation mechanisms.” Moving beyond traditional international relations approaches that treat the Mekong merely as a functional or material arena, this article approaches subregional diplomacy as a fundamentally communicative project. Written from the vantage point of Vietnamese scholarship, the study applies critical discourse analysis, framing analysis, and the strategic narratives approach to 14 official Thai, Vietnamese, and Lao texts, issued mainly in 2025–2026, with Laos’s 2021 development plan as a contextual text. The analysis demonstrates how state actors discursively construct the Mekong as an “intermediary space” to reorganize spatial influence and manage interdependence. Furthermore, it reveals how diplomatic language positions Laos not as a passive geographic buffer but as a “hinge state”: Thai texts tie Thailand’s own plans to Laos’s land-linked strategy, a Vietnam–Laos joint statement frames Lao access to the sea as a shared objective, and Laos’s development plan and Lao state news reports present Laos in that connective role. As such, the article shows that the communicative dimension runs deeply through material mechanisms of mediation, such as logistics, water resources, and non-traditional security, illustrating that modern diplomacy relies as much on the strategic production of meaning as on material capabilities.

title: Audit quality, ESG disclosure and firm performance: Evidence from nonfinancial listed companies in Vietnam
summary: This study examines how audit quality and ESG disclosure relate to the performance of nonfinancial companies listed on the Ho Chi Minh City and Hanoi stock exchanges between 2020 and 2024. Audit quality is captured by Big 4 auditor engagement, auditor change and the type of audit opinion, ESG disclosure is measured with S&P Global ESG scores, and performance is measured by return on assets, return on equity and Tobin's Q. Using pooled OLS, fixed effects and random effects panel regressions, with firm size, age, leverage and the equity to assets ratio as controls, the study finds that results differ across performance measures. Where the Hausman test favours fixed effects, an unqualified audit opinion is positively and significantly associated with both return on equity and Tobin's Q, while leverage is negatively related to return on equity and positively related to Tobin's Q. Neither audit quality nor ESG disclosure is significantly related to return on assets. The positive associations of Big 4 auditors and ESG disclosure with firm value appear only in pooled or random effects estimates and do not persist in the fixed effects models. Auditor change shows no consistent relationship with performance. The findings suggest that audit related signals, rather than ESG scores or auditor size, are most closely linked to shareholder returns and market valuation in Vietnam, although the results are associations and may be affected by endogeneity and measurement limits. The study offers implications for audit oversight and ESG reporting standards in emerging markets.

title: Local Validity Is Not End-to-End Proof
summary: Overview Local validity does not necessarily establish end-to-end consequential validity. A measurement, permission, system trace, or observation may be locally valid without providing sufficient evidence for a broader claim about an outcome. This three-page, non-peer-reviewed research note examines this cross-domain problem through EvidenceToEffect (E2E), using five non-sequential analytical questions: Boundary, Composition, Continuity, Realization, and Resolution. It considers how the scope, composition, continuity, and interpretation of evidence affect the strength of consequential claims. The note also clarifies the relationship between E2E and Execution Governance (EG). E2E addresses whether evidence supports a stated consequential claim, while EG independently addresses current authority to produce governed effects. Their analyses intersect where execution authority is relevant; neither framework is a subset or prerequisite of the other. A conditional U/P analytical comparison distinguishes unsupported affirmative consequential claims from unauthorized committed effects, without treating these as universal measures of E2E. Illustrative examples span measurement, supply chains, software deployment, and security response. Three falsifiable research questions address claim assessability, comparative evaluation against established assurance approaches, and the potential incremental value of governance-specific analysis. Relevant prior work on assurance cases, authorization, claim boundaries, and witnessability is acknowledged. Research scope and limitations This is a conceptual research contribution, not an experimental validation or implementation specification. No new execution protocol, verified comparative superiority, certification, exclusive conceptual priority, or patent clearance is claimed. Related research KU, H. W. (2026). title: Data Elements Driving the Formation of New Quality Productive Forces in Cities: Evidence from 289 Chinese Cities
summary: Data elements are regarded as a new type of production factor that fosters the formation of new quality productive forces in cities and are closely related to sustainable urban development. Drawing on a balanced panel of 289 Chinese cities from 2012 to 2022, this study treats the Big Data Comprehensive Pilot Zone policy as a quasi-natural experiment and employs the difference-in-difference (DID) model. The findings show that this data-element policy designation significantly accelerates the formation of new quality productive forces in cities. Improving the urban business environment and raising the level of urban digital innovation are positively associated with this effect and are consistent with the two proposed channels, although the current design cannot separate direct from indirect effects. The effect of data elements on new quality productive forces in cities is heterogeneous, depending on factors such as urban resource endowments, urban carbon emission intensity, and urban agglomerations. To some extent, the findings serve as a theoretical reference and offer practical implications for sustainable urban development in the era of the digital economy.

title: Islamic Educational Leadership Based on Islamic Epistemology in Responding to the Challenges of the Digital Age for Generation Alpha
summary: Digital transformation calls for Islamic educational leadership grounded in Islamic values to address the challenges faced by Generation Alpha, particularly regarding the validity of information, digital ethics, the protection of learners, and the cultivation of good manners. This study aims to develop a conceptual model of Islamic educational leadership based on Islamic epistemology. The research employs a qualitative approach through a literature review with a conceptual synthesis of the literature on Islamic epistemology, educational leadership, digital transformation, and the learning characteristics of Generation Alpha. Analysis was conducted through the identification of themes, the comparison of theoretical ideas, and the mapping of relationships between concepts. The results of the synthesis produced a model comprising four components: the epistemological foundation; principles of reasoning and decision-making; digital leadership actions; and educational outcome orientation. This model positions the integration of revelation, reason, and empirical experience as the foundation for decision-making, guided by the principles of tabayyun, amanah, justice, and the public good. The conceptual contribution of this research lies in its explanation of the relationship between Islamic epistemology, leaders’ decision-making mechanisms, and digital governance oriented towards learner development. The proposed model remains conceptual in nature and therefore requires empirical testing within Islamic educational institutions.

title: CSR Reporting as Strategic Communication: Financial Reporting Quality and Its Stakeholder Communication Implications
summary: ABSTRACT This study examines the relationship between Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) and Financial Reporting Quality (FRQ) and explores the communication implications of reporting quality improvements. A sequential explanatory mixed‐methods design was employed. In the first stage, survey data from 150 finance professionals employed by London Stock Exchange (LSE)‐listed companies were analysed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS‐SEM). In the second stage, a qualitative content analysis of reports and disclosures from 32 LSE‐listed firms was conducted through the lens of Integrated Marketing Communications (IMC) Theory. The findings indicate that CSR is positively and significantly associated with relevance, faithful representation, understandability, and comparability. The qualitative analysis identified five themes: transparency signals, simplification of information, comparative advantage communication, consistency across platforms, and stakeholder‐centric narratives. These themes illustrate how reporting quality may support communication credibility, message clarity and consistency, stakeholder‐oriented communication, and organizational positioning, while such communication outcomes are interpreted as exploratory implications rather than directly measured effects. The study contributes by positioning financial reporting quality as a communication‐enabling mechanism linking CSR initiatives with stakeholder communication processes and by introducing comparative advantage communication as an interpretive insight emerging from the qualitative findings. The findings offer implications for managers, reporting professionals, and policymakers seeking to enhance transparency, reporting quality, and stakeholder communication.

title: Is It Time to Change the Climate for ESG Investing?
summary: Individual investors have been intrigued by the possibility of merging their personal values with their investing goals for some time. Institutional investors are also increasingly open to considering environmental, social, and governance (ESG) factors when making investment decisions. Prior studies on ESG investing have focused on corporate financial performance, the presence of alpha, and risk mitigation. This study focuses on future stock returns over long-term time horizons. We find largely negative relationships among ESG scores and future stock returns. The analysis also explores returns to alternative combinations of ESG subcomponents (e.g., ES, SG, and EG). The tests of these subcomponent score combinations also reveal negative future return relationships. The results of this and other similar studies are highly dependent on the ESG score database that is used.

title: PRIVATE OPERATOR MANAGEMENT, CORPORATE SOCIAL RESPONSIBILITY, AND VISITOR SATISFACTION IN CAVE TOURISM: A PARALLEL-MEDIATION ANALYSIS OF THE OXALIS PORTFOLIO IN VIETNAM
summary: While private operators increasingly manage ecologically sensitive protected areas, how their management practices relate to visitor satisfaction remains underexplored in cave-tourism research. This study examines a dual parallel mediation model in which Private Operator Management is associated with Visitor Satisfaction, both directly and indirectly through Environmental Conservation Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) and Visitor Environmental Awareness. Data were collected via a 30-item online questionnaire from 317 visitors across seven cave-tour formats operated by Oxalis Adventure Tours in Phong Nha- Kẻ Bàng National Park and Tú Làn, Vietnam, in the 2024-2025 season. SPSS-based analysis validated the measurement model via confirmatory factor analysis and assessed mediation using bootstrapped confidence intervals (5,000 iterations; Hayes, 2018), with the Baron and Kenny (1986) steps retained as a comparability baseline. The model explains 83.2% of the variance in satisfaction; both indirect effects are significant, accounting for 25.9% (CSR) and 22.8% (awareness) of the total effect. An exploratory subgroup analysis is consistent with a crossover: first-time visitors weight the awareness pathway, repeat visitors the CSR pathway. Common-method-variance and discriminant-validity limitations are discussed.

title: Financial Management Practices and Organizational Performance in the Ugandan Public Sector: A Review with Reference to the Ministry of Finance, Planning and Economic Development
summary: Public institutions are entrusted with resources that belong to citizens, and the systems through which those resources are planned, controlled, reported and safeguarded shape whether public money is converted into services and results. This article reviews the literature on the relationship between financial management practices and organizational performance in the public sector, with particular reference to the Ministry of Finance, Planning and Economic Development (MoFPED), Uganda. Through a narrative review of peer-reviewed studies, institutional reports and seminal works, it examines four dimensions of financial management, namely budgeting, financial controls, financial reporting and asset management, and relates them to public-sector performance understood as efficiency in resource utilization, the achievement of planned outputs, the timeliness of service delivery, accountability and the achievement of organizational objectives. The review is anchored in agency theory, stewardship theory and management control theory, and situated within Uganda's public financial management reforms, including the Public Finance Management Act 2015, the Integrated Financial Management System and the successive Public Expenditure and Financial Accountability assessments. The review finds that asset management remains comparatively under-researched and that few studies integrate all four practices within a single ministry, and it concludes that performance depends on the combined and well-implemented operation of the whole financial management system rather than on any practice in isolation.

title: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence on the Performance of Small and Medium Enterprises in Kosovo
summary: Abstract This study investigates the impact of Artificial Intelligence (AI) adoption on the performance of small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in Kosovo, a context where firms face resource constraints but play a pivotal role in economic resilience. Using survey data from 210 SMEs and applying correlation and multiple regression analyses, the research explores how AI integration affects internal management processes, strategic adaptability, and overall organizational outcomes. The objectives were to assess the extent to which AI influences human resource management (HRM), decision-making quality, and customer experience, and to identify enabling factors such as digital readiness and employee training. The findings reveal a strong positive relationship between AI adoption and internal performance indicators, particularly HRM efficiency, where AI training emerged as the strongest predictor of improved outcomes. Decision-making quality was also positively associated with AI, albeit more modestly. However, results indicate a negative relationship between AI usage and customer experience, suggesting that current deployments prioritize internal efficiency at the expense of personalized service delivery. The study concludes that while AI can act as a catalyst for productivity and innovation, its benefits in customer-facing functions remain underutilized. These insights highlight the importance of aligning technological investment with workforce upskilling and customer-centric strategies. The paper contributes to the broader discourse on digital transformation in developing economies by offering recommendations for SME leaders and policymakers to foster inclusive and sustainable AI-driven growth.

title: THE ROLE OF REGULATORY INSTITUTIONS IN PROMOTING EFFECTIVE CORPORATE GOVERNANCE IN UGANDA: A SYSTEMATIC LITERATURE
summary: Corporate governance failures have repeatedly shaped Uganda's financial and public sectors, yet scholarly and professional evidence on how regulatory institutions promote effective governance is scattered across disciplines and source types. This paper reports a systematic literature review, structured around the PRISMA 2020 reporting principles, of 18 sources identified through structured searches of open scholarly, repository, regulatory, professional and law-reporting sources in October 2026. A thematic synthesis, informed by agency theory, stakeholder theory, institutional theory and responsive regulation, yields five findings. First, Uganda's governance architecture is sector-fragmented, combining statutory regulators, line ministries, audit and anti-corruption bodies and a voluntary professional institute without enforcement powers. Second, the most rigorous evidence indicates that codification has outpaced enforcement, with corruption and weak underlying frameworks limiting the effect of codes. Third, reform has been reactive, recurring after bank failures and most recently through the Financial Institutions (Corporate Governance) Regulations 2024. Fourth, evidence on state-owned enterprises is dominated by unpublished case studies reporting weak boards and accountability gaps. Fifth, litigation arising from the Crane Bank takeover shows that regulators' own powers are bounded by statutory procedure and judicial oversight. The review identifies gaps, chiefly the absence of peer-reviewed evaluations of enforcement outcomes, and sets out implications for research, policy and practice. Because the evidence base was assembled from open sources rather than subscription databases, the findings should be treated as a structured, transparent synthesis and not an exhaustive census.

title: AN EXTENDED TECHNOLOGY–ORGANIZATION–ENVIRONMENT (TOE) FRAMEWORK FOR BLOCKCHAIN ADOPTION AMONG SMALL AND MEDIUM ENTERPRISES (SMES)
summary: Blockchain technology offers significant potential to transform business operations through decentralization, transparency, and enhanced security, yet adoption among small and medium enterprises (SMEs) remains notably limited due to technological, organizational, and environmental barriers.This research develops an extended Technology-Organization-Environment (TOE) framework that incorporates blockchain knowledge capability as a distinct construct to address the critical role of organizational awareness, employee expertise, and technological understanding in adoption decisions.The proposed model examines technological factors (perceived benefits, compatibility, complexity, security concerns), organizational factors (top management support, organizational readiness, innovation culture), and environmental factors (regulatory support, competitive pressure, industry support) influencing blockchain adoption.Using a quantitative methodology with structured surveys targeting SME owners, managers, and technology professionals, data will be analyzed through Structural Equation Modelling (SEM) to validate the framework.This study contributes to technology adoption literature by integrating blockchain-specific capabilities into the TOE model while offering practical guidance for researchers, SME managers, policymakers, and solution providers to develop strategies that reduce adoption barriers, improve organizational readiness, and accelerate blockchain-enabled digital transformation among SMEs.

title: Directors Liability in the Collapse of Financial Institutions: A Legal Analysis of the Position in Uganda
summary: The collapse of a financial institution raises demands for accountability, but institutional failure does not itself establish a director's personal liability. This article examines the relationship between directors' duties, bank resolution and the enforcement of remedies in Uganda. It adopts a structured documentary review and doctrinal analysis of legislation, regulations, reported judgments and selected institutional and scholarly materials. Particular attention is given to differences between original and revised statutory numbering, the Financial Institutions (Corporate Governance) Regulations 2024 and their 2025 amendment. The analysis distinguishes liability for a director's own misconduct from the exceptional disregard of corporate personality, and separates supervisory sanctions from compensatory recovery and criminal proceedings. The Crane Bank litigation demonstrates the importance of litigation capacity, the legal stage of intervention and the distinction between corporate existence and a banking licence. Other Ugandan decisions illustrate the need to prove misconduct and identify the proper procedural route. Comparative reasoning on creditor interests supplies a limited benchmark rather than a substitute for Ugandan law. The article finds that Uganda has substantial substantive duties, while effective accountability depends on preserving evidence, identifying an authorized claimant, attributing conduct to individual directors and connecting breach to a legally recoverable loss. It recommends clearer coordination between resolution and litigation, stronger records preservation, reasoned enforcement decisions and transparent reporting of completed recovery proceedings. The contribution is a framework for assessing director accountability without treating every bank failure as fraud or every procedural dismissal as a determination of the underlying allegations.

title: Fostering Change Championing Behavior in Public Institutions: The Interplay of Digital Leadership, Transactional Leadership, and Agile Organizational Culture
summary: Abstract Digital transformation and increasingly complex external environmental dynamics are driving public institutions, including the police, to adopt adaptive and strategic leadership approaches. This study aims to examine the direct and indirect effects of Digital Leadership and Transactional Leadership on Change Championing Behaviour, with Agile Organisational Culture as a mediating variable. Using a descriptive and exploratory quantitative approach, primary data were collected from 118 police personnel from Indonesia through structured questionnaires and analysed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLSSEM) with the assistance of SmartPLS 3.3.3. The results revealed that both leadership styles have a significant influence on champion behaviour towards change, with Digital Leadership showing a stronger influence in shaping an agile organisational culture. Additionally, Agile Organizational Culture was found to partially mediate the relationship between the two leadership styles and Change Championing Behaviour, with mediation values of 47.55% and 38.45%, respectively. These findings confirm that the success of organisational transformation in the public sector heavily depends on the synergy between strategic leadership and adaptive work culture. This study provides practical implications for policymakers to design leadership development programmes and organisational culture revitalisation initiatives to enhance the responsiveness and readiness of public institutions in facing disruptions in the digital era.

title: Prioritization of quality management system criteria in shipyard operations: A fuzzy AHP–TOPSIS case from the Marmara Region of Türkiye
summary: Quality management systems (QMSs) play an important role in guaranteeing efficiency, consistency, and continuous improvement in production processes. The application of structured quality management frameworks is significant in the shipyard sector. The structured application of QMS frameworks—such as ISO 9001—can lead to significant improvements in quality control. This study aims to prioritize QMS-related criteria and tools applicable to shipyard operations using a hybrid fuzzy analytic hierarchy process and TOPSIS methodology. Expert evaluations, a literature review, and multi-criteria decision-making methods are all part of the structure of the study. According to the results of the study, the most influential sub-criteria in the successful implementation of quality management are strategic planning and organizational structure. Moreover, control charts were identified as the most effective quality management tool for maintaining consistent quality levels among the tools examined. Additionally, the study emphasized the critical role of digital transformation and Industry 4.0 technologies in enhancing the implementation of quality management performance. This research adds to the increasing amount of information on quality management in industrial production and provides useful suggestions for shipyards looking for ways to maximize their quality management practices.

title: Ethical leadership as an informal HR governance mechanism: linking ethical leadership to organizational citizenship behavior via trust and affective commitment
summary: Purpose This study examines how ethical leadership activates organizational citizenship behavior through trust and affective commitment, and how these relational processes are shaped within the context of ethical climate. Design/methodology/approach This study uses a cross-sectional survey design with data from 1,096 technical employees in 42 Turkish manufacturing and technology firms. Ethical leadership, trust, affective commitment, ethical climate, and organizational citizenship behavior were measured with validated Likert scales. Hypotheses were tested using structural equation modeling (DWLS) and conditional process analyses (Hayes PROCESS), estimating direct, indirect, and moderated effects and assessing measurement quality (reliability/validity) and potential common method bias. Findings The findings show that ethical leadership has both direct and indirect effects on organizational citizenship behavior. Trust and affective commitment function as complementary psychosocial mechanisms in the transformation of ethical leadership into behavioral outcomes, while ethical climate reshapes the strength of these mechanisms depending on the context. Originality/value The study conceptualizes ethical leadership as an informal ethical governance mechanism and tests a context-sensitive model in which trust and affective commitment transmit ethical signals to citizenship behavior under varying ethical climates. It advances prior work by integrating governance logic with social learning and social exchange perspectives, demonstrating how ethical climate reshapes the strength of relational mechanisms. Evidence from a large multi-firm sample in a developing economy undergoing digital transformation extends the contextual generalizability of ethical leadership research.

title: The concept of reliability of financial reporting: past, present, and future
summary: The article presents a comparative analysis of the concept of reliability of accounting (financial) statements based on contemporary scholarly research, from the perspective of the evolution of Russian and international legislation. The object of the study is the financial reporting of enterprises and organizations; the subject of the study is the concept of reliability of such reporting. The purpose and objectives of the research are to identify the historical foundations of the concept of reliability, to examine and analyze the terminology of reliability in modern Russian accounting legislation and in accordance with IFRS standards, to identify the problems associated with the implementation of an integrated reporting approach for economic entities in Russia and abroad, and to analyze the prospects for changes in methods of assessing the reliability of financial reporting and the transformation of the concept of reliability itself in the context of digitalization of the economy and the development of artificial intelligence. The methodological basis of the study consists of retrospective, systemic-functional, and comparative analyses, as well as a predictive assessment of development prospects.

title: Artificial intelligence's effect on financial reports for listed banks in Saudi Arabia
summary: Objectives: This study investigated the impact of artificial intelligence (AI) on financial accounting practices in banks listed on the Saudi Stock Exchange (Tadawul), focusing on system integration, reporting accuracy, information interpretation, and presentation quality within a survey-based empirical context. It also considered the perceived benefits and challenges of AI adoption in the Saudi banking sector. Method: The study employed a quantitative, survey-based design, using primary data collected through a structured questionnaire administered to accountants, auditors, financial analysts, and managers in Saudi banks. Data were analyzed using SPSS, and reliability testing showed strong internal consistency, with Cronbach’s alpha values ranging from 0.889 to 0.931. Results: The findings indicated statistically significant positive associations between AI adoption and all examined dimensions of financial accounting practices, with correlation coefficients ranging from 0.54 to 0.87 (p <.01). Conclusion: The study provided empirical evidence from a survey-based investigation indicating that AI adoption was associated with improvements in the quality and efficiency of financial reporting in Saudi banks. These results reflected perceived relationships rather than causal effects, contributing to the limited literature on AI in financial accounting in emerging markets and offering practical implications for policymakers and banking leaders.

title: Integrating Internet of Things and Blockchain Technology in Accounting Information Systems: Opportunities, Challenges, and Implications for Accounting Information Quality
summary: The swift advancement of digital technology has generated novel prospects for enhancing the efficiency of Accounting Information Systems (AIS). Among these innovations, the Internet of Things (IoT) and blockchain has significant capacity to revolutionize the gathering, processing, validation, and dissemination of accounting data. The Internet of Things facilitates the automatic and real-time collection of operational data through interconnected devices and sensors, whereas blockchain offers a communal, immutable ledger of transactions that enhances traceability and accountability. Incorporating these technologies could enhance the promptness, dependability, clarity, and verifiability of financial data. This study explores the prospective amalgamation of IoT and blockchain in Accounting Information Systems, concentrating on inventory accounting, fixed-asset oversight, transaction validation, financial reporting, and ongoing auditing. It employs a theoretical research methodology grounded in an examination of pertinent scholarly literature. The document also highlights significant obstacles to adoption, including as cybersecurity threats, data privacy issues, costs of implementation, interoperability, regulatory obligations, and the dependability of information gathered from physical devices. The article suggests a cohesive structure where IoT devices document operational occurrences, blockchain maintains authenticated transaction records, and the AIS compiles accounting entries and produces financial statements. The research determines that the integration of IoT and blockchain could enhance the quality of accounting information, contingent upon the implementation of suitable internal controls, governance structures, and expert supervision.

title: ESG media buzz and firm performance: the moderating effect of firms’ strategic emphasis
summary: While firms increasingly invest in Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) initiatives, stakeholders’ awareness of these efforts depends largely on external communication. Prior research focuses on the performance implications of ESG practices themselves, overlooking the role of ESG-related media visibility. This study examines how ESG media buzz links to firm value and risk. Analysing publicly listed US food and beverage firms, the results reveal an inverted U-shaped relationship between ESG media buzz and firm value, which weakens when firms strategically prioritise value appropriation over value creation. Additionally, ESG media buzz exhibits a U-shaped relationship with firm risk. These findings highlight the strategic importance of understanding externally mediated ESG visibility and its interpretation in capital markets.

title: It is all about digitalization: investigating antecedents and effects of digital transformation
summary: Abstract Digital transformation is increasingly recognized as a vital driver of competitiveness, yet the precise organizational factors that most strongly influence its success remain ambiguous. This study addresses this gap by examining how strategic, operational, organizational, and cultural factors jointly relate to digital transformation outcomes, and by uncovering the mediating role of innovation success in shaping overall company success. Drawing upon data from 279 organizational key informants in Germany with substantive involvement in digital transformation, this study develops a holistic framework that not only identifies key organizational factors relevant for digital transformation success but also compares their associations with transformation success when considered simultaneously. The findings reveal numerically larger associations for cultural and operational factors, whereas strategic and organizational factors exhibit smaller coefficients, with the organizational-domain association only marginally significant ( p < 0.10). Although bootstrap-based parameter-difference tests do not support a statistically established ranking of the four domains, the results underline the relevance of all four domains while suggesting that cultural and operational conditions may warrant particular attention depending on firms’ specific transformation context. Furthermore, the results reveal a significant indirect association between digital transformation success and company success through innovation success, accounting for around 60% of the total association in the specified model. Hence, organizations seeking to maximize the returns on their digital initiatives should consider cultural and operational conditions alongside the strategic and organizational foundations of digital transformation. Taken together, these insights offer actionable guidance for businesses aiming to allocate their resources strategically, consider cultural and operational conditions as important diagnostic starting points, and harness the full potential of digital transformation through a concerted emphasis on innovation.

title: TSMC, discrimination litigation and sustainability reporting
summary: Research methodology This case was developed using secondary data sources. Primary case materials were drawn from official public filings, specifically TSMC’s annual Form 20-F and sustainability reports, both publicly accessible online. Supplementary context was gathered from news coverage and publicly available media coverage on TSMC’s US operations. Applicable financial reporting standards, specifically International Accounting Standard (IAS) 37, Provisions, Contingent Liabilities and Contingent Assets, issued by the International Accounting Standards Board (IASB) and industry-specific disclosure standards issued by the Sustainability Accounting Standards Board (SASB) were also consulted and are included as appendices to the case.Instructor Note on SASB/ISSB Governance: SASB is no longer an independent organization. In August 2022, the Value Reporting Foundation, which housed SASB, was consolidated into the IFRS Foundation, and responsibility for the SASB Standards transferred to the International Sustainability Standards Board (ISSB). The industry-based SASB Standards remain in use and are now maintained by the ISSB. For simplicity and to facilitate students’ reading and research, the terms “SASB” and “SASB Standards” are retained throughout the case and teaching note.The protagonist, Wen-Chang Hao, is a composite character created for teaching purposes. Her title, responsibilities and organizational position are based on the publicly available LinkedIn profile of an individual holding a comparable role within TSMC’s sustainability function, as well as TSMC’s public sustainability disclosures and corporate governance documentation. No individual by this name has been identified as holding this position at TSMC, and the character’s deliberations and decisions are constructed for pedagogical purposes rather than drawn from any primary or firsthand source. Case overview/synopsis Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC), the world’s largest semiconductor foundry with over 70% global market share, confronted a disclosure decision as Wen-Chang Hao, Global Sustainability Engagement and Strategy Manager, drafted the company’s 2025 Sustainability Report for its internal May 2026 deadline. Two active US class-action lawsuits had emerged against TSMC’s US operations: one alleging racial and national-origin discrimination involving more than 30 plaintiffs in the Arizona plant, and a second filed in April 2026 alleging systemic gender discrimination potentially affecting thousands of current and former female employees. Neither lawsuit had been identified as a named legal contingency in TSMC’s most recently submitted Form 20-F.Hao’s decision represented a double materiality problem. Financial reporting standards permitted the omission of both lawsuits in the absence of a reliable damage estimate, while TSMC’s voluntary sustainability/ESG frameworks created no binding obligation to disclose. Yet the gap between the two reporting channels, one silent on workforce litigation, the other publicly celebrating global sustainability/ESG leadership, raised substantive questions that Hao had to resolve: whether to acknowledge the pending litigation in the 2025 Sustainability Report, at what level of specificity and in which sections, and how to frame any disclosure relative to the annual report and financial statement’s treatment of the same matters. Complexity academic level This case addresses loss contingency recognition, materiality judgment and ESG disclosure across financial and nonfinancial reporting channels. It is appropriate for upper-level undergraduate and graduate courses, depending on the depth of analysis and instructor emphasis. It is suitable for courses including Intermediate Accounting, Auditing, Sustainability Accounting and Human Resource Management. It may also be used in International Business courses, particularly in discussions of multinational reporting environments and the cross-functional implications of workforce-related challenges and risks. The case is recommended for use mid-to-late in the term, after students have been introduced to either contingent liability standards (in accounting courses) or stakeholder theory and materiality frameworks (in Sustainability/ESG or IB courses).The case was pilot-tested in an undergraduate International Business course with approximately 25 students majoring in accounting, finance or management participating in the discussion. Student engagement and feedback informed subsequent refinements to the case materials and teaching notes.

title: Reconstruction of Islamic Green Banking: Fiqh Al-Bi’ah As A Model Of Sustainable Islamic Finance
summary: Despite the growth of green financing, Islamic banking remains largely reliant on secular Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) frameworks, overlooking the normative foundations of Fiqh al-Bi’ah (Islamic environmental jurisprudence). This study reconstructs an Islamic green banking model grounded in Fiqh al-Bi’ah to advance Sustainable Islamic Finance. Using a qualitative socio-legal approach, it combines bibliometric analysis, Natural Language Processing (NLP), and Ijtihadi Maqashidi analysis to examine 34 Indonesian Islamic banks from 2017 to 2024. NLP-based text mining reveals isomorphic mimicry, with Fiqh al-Bi’ah terminology appearing in less than 1% of sustainability reports. In response, the study proposes an operational model integrating principles such as fasād, mīzān, and ḥimā into banking mechanisms, including Eco-Haram Screening, Maqasid-based Credit Scoring, and Conservation-Linked Financing. The model offers a framework for regulators and Sharia standard-setters to shift Islamic banking from compliance-based practices toward value-based sustainable finance.

title: A cross-cycle water-accounting vulnerability in NHANES: a paired audit of a published mortality exposure
summary: Background. Zhou et al. (2022) reported inverse associations of dietary water-source intake with mortality in 35,463 NHANES participants from 1999–2014. Beginning in 2005–2006, NHANES recorded plain drinking water as itemised intake and included it in total dietary moisture. We examined whether a literal implementation of the published exposure definitions could add this water twice. Methods. We compared CDC dietary-total and item-level records across eight NHANES cycles and constructed two source-water definitions in the same screened sample (N = 35,163). One followed a potentially duplicative literal residual; the other removed post-2005 plain water from the residual exactly once. We examined cycle discontinuities, distributional proximity to Zhou et al.'s published summary, and quartile reassignment. Exploratory mortality analyses used a distinct, non-equivalent Cox model with NCHS public-use follow-up through 2019. New robustness analyses refitted the archived model after restricting survey cycles to 2003–2014, with and without requiring a valid second-day recall. Results. The original article's exposure definitions imply the potentially duplicative M + P construction unless an unreported harmonisation step was used. In 101,153 matched person-days, item-moisture sums reconciled with the reported aggregate to numerical precision. The literal versus corrected definitions yielded paired-sample median food-water residuals of 949 versus 556 g/day; the published Zhou median was 924 g/day. The vulnerable reconstruction created a post-2005 jump in median apparent food-water share from approximately 21% to 41–46%; the non-duplicative calculation remained approximately 20–25%. In the pooled exploratory 2019 model (31,046 participants; 5,898 deaths), the Q4/Q1 hazard ratios were 0.910 (95% CI 0.805–1.029) and 0.979 (0.883–1.085). In the 2003–2014 restricted cohort they were 0.984 and 1.014; with only valid second-day recalls, 1.026 and 1.046. All corresponding intervals included 1. A complete 48-row archive of exploratory model fits also includes materially different specifications, and cannot support a stable mortality-effect claim. Conclusions. The literal post-2005 accounting vulnerability and large exposure-classification differences are demonstrable. Similarity of a vulnerable reconstruction to published marginal distributions raises a specific implementation concern, but Zhou et al.'s actual code is unavailable; we cannot establish that the original authors made that error. The mortality-model difference in our audit is exploratory and sensitive to survey-era and recall-completeness choices; it is not a corrected estimate of the original published association.

title: The Role of Artificial Intelligence in Improving Accounting and Auditing Practices: A Study of Selected Organizations in Uganda
summary: This systematic literature review (SLR) synthesises evidence on how artificial intelligence (AI) is improving accounting and auditing practice, with specific attention to selected organizations in Uganda: audit and accountancy firms, public-sector accounting entities, small and medium-sized practices, and the professional body. The review followed PRISMA 2020 and an a priori protocol. Peer-reviewed and professional-body sources published from 2015 onward were identified through multi-database searching and citation chasing, screened against explicit criteria, appraised with the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT) and an adapted checklist for conceptual papers, and analysed through thematic synthesis. Nineteen studies were included. This systematic literature review found that: (1) documented applications and benefits; (2) low and uneven adoption, especially in Uganda; (3) technology, organizational and environmental determinants of adoption; (4) skills, education and workforce effects; and (5) ethics, governance and regulation. Ugandan evidence is limited to one survey of professional accountants and one conference study of public-sector readiness; no study measured audit-quality or cost outcomes of AI in a Ugandan organization. Most evidence relies on perception data from single-country cross-sections. Implications: Regulators, firms and educators should prioritise skills, governance and affordable tooling; researchers should pursue organization-level, longitudinal and outcome-based designs. Originality: To our knowledge, this is the first SLR focused on AI in accounting and auditing in Uganda.

title: Mapping highly cited research in FT50 journals: a bibliometric and science-mapping analysis
summary: Purpose The Financial Times 50 (FT50) journal list is a prestigious and influential ranking, widely regarded as a benchmark of excellence in business and economics research. The purpose of the present study was to identify trends and examine the 50 most-cited bibliometric analyses to gain insights into influential publications in management and economics. Design/methodology/approach The Scopus database was used to comprehensively identify the most-cited documents in FT50 journals without year or language restriction. The 50 most-cited publications were retrieved from each of the 50 journals included in the 2016 FT50 list, yielding a corpus of 2,500 publications, which were downloaded in CSV format. Documents were evaluated for various characteristics, including year of publication, document type, names of authors, topic, open access and affiliations. Findings The results found that the MIS Quarterly: Management Information Systems has received the highest citations. Trailblazing researchers such as Shleifer A., Mackenzie S.B. and Podsakoff PM exhibit high citation strength and centrality in co-authorship networks. The study also reveals that University of California was the most productive institution, majority of the institutions were from the USA. Major topics of interest in the top 50 most-cited papers were corporate governance, supply chain management, earnings management and entrepreneurship. Originality/value The study covers to understanding the impact of researchers of FT50 authors and offers insights for academics, organizations and policymakers aiming into the evolution of high-impact business research.

title: PEDAGOGICAL POTENTIAL OF BENCHMARKING IN THE CONDITIONS OF DIGITAL TRANSFORMATION OF EDUCATION
summary: Relevance of the Study. The article is devoted to highlighting the problem of pedagogical potential of benchmarking in the conditions of digital transformation of education. The relevance of the research is determined by the need to find effective mechanisms for ensuring the quality of education in the conditions of active implementation of digital technologies and the formation of the digital educational space of higher education institutions. It has been established that the digitalization of education contributes to the modernization of the content, forms and methods of education, the expansion of access to educational resources, the development of digital competences and the improvement of educational communication. The purpose of the article was to substantiate the pedagogical potential of benchmarking in the conditions of digital transformation of education, to reveal the peculiarities of the implementation of the benchmarking approach to increasing the efficiency and quality of the educational process. To achieve this goal, methods of analysis, synthesis, generalisation, and systematisation of scientific sources were employed. Research Methods. The study employed theoretical methods, including analysis, synthesis, generalisation, and systematisation of scholarly and regulatory sources on educational digitalisation, digital transformation, quality assurance, and benchmarking. Comparative analysis was used to examine international experience and to identify opportunities and barriers related to digital benchmarking in education. Results. Benchmarking was defined as a systematic process of searching for, analysing, comparing, and adapting effective educational practices. The analysis showed that digital platforms, cloud services, open educational resources, electronic databases, and professional networks expand opportunities to compare educational practices, disseminate innovation, support teachers' professional development, and improve educational content and organisation. The study also identified implementation barriers in Ukraine, including uneven digital infrastructure, limited resources, insufficient awareness of benchmarking methodology, and the absence of systematic mechanisms for sharing effective practices. Conclusions. Benchmarking has considerable pedagogical potential as a quality improvement tool in a digitally transformed educational environment. Its effective use requires critical adaptation rather than mechanical transfer of external practices. Further development should focus on methodological guidance, evaluation criteria, professional educational networks, international cooperation, and national mechanisms for disseminating effective educational practices

title: Designing a Gamified Tool: An ADDIE Approach to Capital Market Flashcard Development
summary: Traditional, lecture-based finance courses frequently overwhelm undergraduate students with dense theoretical content, leading to poor knowledge retention, lower overall engagement, and a heavy reliance on last-minute cramming before major assessments. To address these persistent educational challenges, this study details the design, development, and implementation of a mobile-friendly digital flashcard game specifically tailored for an undergraduate Financial Markets and Institutions (FIN) course using the systematic ADDIE instructional design framework. By integrating active recall strategies, custom visual aids, and an algorithm-driven Spaced Repetition System (SRS), the platform transforms passive studying into a dynamic learning process that prompts students to systematically review challenging concepts based on their individual mastery levels. Subject-matter experts rigorously vetted the curriculum content for accuracy and practical relevance prior to deployment, while formative evaluations directly measured student usability, overall engagement, and conceptual comprehension during active coursework. Formative findings, including high expert ratings for content validity and evidence of adaptive scheduling from system logs, suggest that the tool has strong potential to support active recall. However, its effectiveness in improving long-term knowledge retention and reducing academic anxiety will be examined in a subsequent summative evaluation. Ultimately, by documenting the comprehensive analysis, design, and development phases, this study provides instructional designers and finance educators with a practical, replicable blueprint for implementing gamified, technology-enhanced active learning tools across complex capital markets curricula.

title: ESG Performance and Financial Outcomes in the Hospitality Industry: A Systematic Literature Review
summary: ABSTRACT Corporate social responsibility (CSR) and ESG are in the spotlight in hospitality management research; however, the CSR/ESG body of knowledge is fragmented by incompatible measurement approaches. Most of this work has been conducted at the regional level, with little to no attention to governance issues. To date, no study has combined a systematic review of the CSR/ESG literature in the hospitality industry with a pre‐registered design incorporating bibliometric analysis and a meta‐analytic approach. The main objectives are to map the research landscape on ESG/CSR to financial performance linkages for the hospitality industry (RQ1), to evaluate the combined strength of association and the direction of the ESG‐to‐performance linkage along with the structural moderators of this relationship through a meta‐analytic approach (RQ2), and to integrate the primary mediation processes, moderation variables, and research gaps, particularly about the governance dimension (RQ3). Peer‐reviewed empirical studies, along with non‐empirical studies, that have examined ESG or CSR as an independent variable and financial performance as a dependent variable for hospitality sector firms (hotels, restaurants, casino hotels, cruise lines, and resort complexes), limiting the language to English and the publication period to 2010 to 2026. We searched the Web of Science Core Collection and Scopus on January 12, 2026. We used six parallel search strings to address all three research questions, covering ESG/CSR, hospitality, and financial performance. Sensitivity was 100% because the search retrieved all 12 pre‐identified gold‐standard studies. Results showed a substantial duplication rate (49.6%) between the two databases. The protocol was registered with the Open Science Framework (OSF) before data collection (V5; all amendments were filed before each analytical stage). We assessed the empirical studies using a hybrid of the Newcastle‐Ottawa Scale (NOS, max 9) and a custom five‐item Econometric Quality Checklist. Risk‐of‐bias (RoB) inter‐rater reliability ( N = 47 dual‐reviewed studies, 50% verification sample) reached Po = 83.5% and Cohen's κ = 0.791 after resolving discrepancies, satisfying the pre‐registered ≥ 80% Po and ≥ 0.60 κ thresholds. All 47 RoB weight category assignments reached full agreement. Literature review studies were assessed using A Measurement Tool to Assess Systematic Reviews AMSTAR‐2. Ninety‐five studies included in total (72 empirical, 23 non‐empirical). K = 23 studies ( k = 84 effect sizes) were eligible for meta‐analytic pooling. The primary three‐level multilevel random‐effects model yielded r = 0.211 (95% CI [0.103, 0.314], p = 0.0001; I 2 = 93.3%). The one‐per‐study model yielded r = 0.216 (95% CI [0.106, 0.320], p = 0.0001). Restricting the pool to objective third‐party ESG ratings yielded r = 0.061 ( p = 0.195), while self‐reported CSR surveys yielded r = 0.353 ( p < 0.001). Funnel asymmetry was detected (Egger's test: z = 2.732, p = 0.013), but trim‐and‐fill imputed zero missing studies; PET‐PEESE bias‐corrected estimates are non‐significant, consistent with measurement‐type heterogeneity rather than suppression bias. The governance ESG dimension yielded r = −0.023 from five studies. SciMat longitudinal co‐word analysis confirmed the ESG cluster growing from marginal (centrality = 8.37, P1) to structurally prominent (centrality = 17.71, P4), with the CSR‐to‐ESG terminological transition underway but still incomplete. The positive ESG‐to‐financial‐performance association in the hospitality industry is entirely dependent on measurement: objective third‐party ratings show no detectable association, whereas self‐reported property‐level CSR measures show a large positive effect. This divergence is a structurally diagnostic finding that generates two competing hypotheses: the construct validity hypothesis (enterprise‐level and property‐level ESG instruments target theoretically distinct constructs with different pathways to financial performance) and the methodological account (common method bias inflates self‐reported estimates), which cannot be disentangled because the ESG measurement approach and study design are fully collinear in the pool. The governance dimension is the field's primary intellectual deficit, established convergently across three evidence streams (bibliometric, thematic, researcher self‐report) and consistent with the meta‐analytic arm ( r = −0.023, K = 5), which is too sparse to estimate the relationship reliably and is itself a structural signal of the deficit. The primary value‐creation mechanisms, corporate reputation, competitive advantage, and ESG as organizational insurance during crises, are theoretically coherent but causally underidentified.

title: CENTRAL BANK DIGITAL CURRENCY: A NEW INFRASTRUCTURE FOR THE DIGITAL ECONOMY
summary: Tiền kỹ thuật số quốc gia (Central Bank Digital Currency - CBDC) đang được nhiều ngân hàng trung ương nghiên cứu trong bối cảnh hạ tầng tài chính phải thích ứng với sự phát triển của thanh toán xuyên biên giới, tài sản được token hóa và các quy trình giao dịch ngày càng tự động hóa. Bài viết nhằm phân tích sự thay đổi về vai trò của CBDC từ góc độ hạ tầng tài chính, tập trung làm rõ những yêu cầu mới của nền kinh tế số đối với hoạt động thanh toán, quyết toán và những năng lực mà CBDC, đặc biệt là CBDC bán buôn, có thể bổ sung cho hệ thống hiện có. Nghiên cứu sử dụng phương pháp phân tích tài liệu định tính, kết hợp tổng hợp, so sánh và đối sánh ba sáng kiến quốc tế gồm Agorá, Rialto và Acacia theo một số tiêu chí chung. Kết quả phân tích cho thấy các sáng kiến về CBDC đang tập trung vào ba hướng chính: tăng cường khả năng tương tác trong thanh toán và quyết toán xuyên biên giới; hỗ trợ tự động hóa các quy trình thanh toán; và kết nối CBDC với các thị trường tài sản được token hóa. Trên cơ sở đó, bài viết cho rằng giá trị của CBDC không chỉ nằm ở việc số hóa tiền ngân hàng trung ương mà còn ở khả năng mở rộng năng lực của hạ tầng tài chính trong những môi trường giao dịch mới. Đóng góp của nghiên cứu là đề xuất cách tiếp cận xem CBDC như một thành phần của kiến trúc hạ tầng tài chính đang được định hình trong nền kinh tế số. Tuy nhiên, các kết quả chủ yếu dựa trên tài liệu thứ cấp và các dự án liên quan đến CBDC bán buôn đang trong giai đoạn nghiên cứu hoặc thử nghiệm, do đó chưa thể suy rộng trực tiếp cho mọi mô hình CBDC.
