title: Integrating strategic marketing and ESG compliance management for balanced enterprise development under CSRD regimes: a dynamic capabilities approach
summary: Grounded in Dynamic Capabilities Theory, this study investigates whether compliance management enables environmental, social, and governance (ESG) strategies to transcend symbolic greenwashing and deliver substantive ecological impacts aligned with UN SDGs 12 and 13 under the EU Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD) regime. Utilizing a two-way fixed-effects panel regression, this research analyzes an empirical sample of STOXX Europe 600 companies over the regulatory transition period (2022–2025). Data from LSEG and Bloomberg databases strictly measure non-financial environmental performance, specifically absolute greenhouse gas (GHG) Scopes 1, 2, and 3 emissions, and waste recycling ratios. The empirical analysis reveals that high-level compliance management significantly enhances corporate environmental strategy efficacy. Crucially, ESG dynamic capabilities (eco-design and resource reduction) fully mediate this relationship, transmuting rigid compliance frameworks into operational routines that yield absolute reductions in GHG emissions and improved waste recovery, thereby facilitating genuine ecological decoupling. Diverging from the financial focus of ESG literature, this study re-centers the narrative on "impact materiality." It establishes a novel framework proving that the ultimate value of corporate sustainability lies in verifiable ecological preservation, advancing the scholarship on sustainable development and CSRD compliance.

title: Proper working-time accounting as a safeguard for employees’ occupational health and safety
summary: Abstract Every employee has the right to working conditions that respect their health, safety, and dignity. Working time is a condition of employment and is subject to restrictions to safeguard employees’ occupational health and safety. EU Member States are obliged to ensure that these restrictions are observed in employment relationships. Compliance with working-time restrictions can be ensured through working-time accounting. The corresponding obligation is imposed on employers, who are expected to establish an objective, reliable, and accessible system for accounting for working time. This article examines how to create a working-time accounting system that meets the above conditions and protects employees’ health and safety. To calculate working time, it is essential to understand the various ways in which it can be determined. An “always-on” work culture and the blurring of boundaries between working and rest time complicate working-time accounting. The absence of national regulation may lead employers to assume that it is sufficient to measure working time at their own discretion. This approach creates inequality at the national level and fails to foster a favourable environment for protecting workers’ health, safety, and dignity. In this article, the authors present their view of how a working-time accounting system should be designed to ensure safeguards for employees’ occupational health and safety. The article is based on an analysis of European Union, Spanish, German, Greek, and Estonian regulations.

title: “The Minimum Wage Is the Maximum Wage”: How Goal Replacement Perpetuates Means–Ends Decoupling
summary: This research examines how organizations contribute to the perpetuation of means–ends decoupling (MED) within issue-based fields organized around societal problems, under conditions of heightened field scrutiny. In such settings, organizations often profess commitment to field goals and visibly comply with institutionally prescribed practices to satisfy monitoring, reporting, and public evaluation requirements. However, many adopted goals remain underachieved, raising questions about how compliance without progress endures and how claims of commitment remain credible under transparency regimes intended to spur substantive goal pursuit. Our data came from 75 interviews with 68 brands, suppliers, and third-party organizations pursuing worker well-being in global fashion supply chains. We unveil auditability-based goal replacement as an organizational-level mechanism through which actors rhetorically foreground compliance as public evidence of commitment while narrowing internal goal pursuit to auditable thresholds that serve their core goals, thereby allowing shortfalls to persist. Self-silencing about this substitution and the instrumentalizing of shortfalls close the configuration into a self-reinforcing loop. The study advances MED scholarship by (i) showing how organizations leverage field conditions and appropriate the existing scrutiny infrastructures to advance their core goals while reproducing the means–ends gap, (ii) problematizing the authenticity of commitment claims, and (iii) explaining how goal-ineffective compliance prevails as a credible substitute for adopted goals. It also extends research on organizational responses to institutional complexity and calls for greater attention to institutional impact—that is, the realized advancement of the societal aim an institution emerged to address.

title: ENVIRONMENTAL, SOCIAL, AND GOVERNANCE (ESG) DISCLOSURE ON CORPORATE VALUE AND MODERATED BY PROFIT GROWTH IN THE LISTED BANKING SECTOR ON THE INDONESIA STOCK EXCHANGE (2022-2025)
summary: The development of Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) Disclosure practices is increasingly important in the banking sector because it is not only related to corporate transparency and sustainability but also can influence investor perceptions of corporate value. This study aims to analyze the influence of Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) Disclosure on corporate value and analyze the role of profit growth in moderating this relationship in banking sector companies listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange for the period 2022–2025. This study uses a quantitative approach with secondary data obtained from annual reports and corporate sustainability reports. The sample was determined using a purposive sampling technique and obtained 27 banking companies with an observation period of four years. Data analysis was conducted using panel data regression with the help of EViews 12 and Moderated Regression Analysis (MRA). The results show that ESG disclosure has a positive and significant effect on firm value. Profit growth also has a positive and significant effect on firm value. Furthermore, profit growth moderates the relationship between ESG disclosure and firm value by strengthening this positive effect. The findings of this study indicate that ESG disclosure supported by strong profit growth can increase investor confidence and contribute significantly to increasing the value of banking companies.

title: A Loose Ceiling, Not a Certificate: Auditing Fisher-Separability Bounds on Hallucination Detectability Across Architectures
summary: Status: Manuscript (preprint). Can the ceiling on hallucination detectability be read off a representation before any probe is trained? Fisher separability J yields a closed-form, training-free value that empirically upper-bounds linear-probe AUROC via the binormal identity Φ(√(J/2)). Rerunning six models (GPT-2 117M/Medium, Qwen2.5 0.5B–7B) under one matched real-generation pipeline, we find the bound is never violated but badly loose: it over-predicts probe AUROC by 0.32–0.41 under exact-match/F1 labels (and 0.18–0.30 under an independent semantic judge, at re-selected layers). The central question is how much of that gap is the estimator rather than the representation, and the answer is: most of it. Under a label-permutation null on the same activations – no class signal by construction – the estimator still returns a "certificate" of 0.87–0.94 for GPT-2 117M, GPT-2 Medium and Qwen2.5-0.5B, which against their same-layer probe AUROCs of 0.55–0.56 is 86–92% of the gap we report for those three models. Observed J exceeds its null at p < 0.001–0.045 uncorrected for four of six models, and is not distinguishable from random labels at all for the other two (p=0.195, 0.380). Holding all 38 significance tests in the paper to one Holm-Bonferroni family leaves 3 surviving. We also retract an invariance claim from an earlier version of this work: an apparent rotation-sensitivity of Ĵ, which we had read as a basis-dependence of fixed-rank truncation, traces entirely to an unseeded randomized SVD and vanishes under a deterministic solver. We report the null control and the determinism check as the two diagnostics any Fisher-style detectability ceiling should carry – offered here because they overturned our own headline rather than confirmed it. title: PACEGuard: Minimum Evidence-Cut Auditing for Polluted-Evidence Fragility in LLM SOC Agents
summary: Abstract LLM-assisted SOC agents can base verdicts and high-impact actions on polluted or weak-lineage evidence. We frame this dependence as a graph intervention problem. PACEGuard wraps an LLM SOC reasoner with MECI, which searches for the lowest-cost structurally valid evidence cut that changes a verdict, citation set, or action. The resulting empirical fragility score routes cheap-to-flip cases to sanitization or review, while respecting source boundaries, lineage, temporal order, semantic retrieval, and independent corroboration. We separate a formal property for an additive bounded-influence model from the measured black-box score. On a fixed-seed benchmark with 2,400 clean cases and 12,000 polluted variants, PACEGuard lowers attack success rate (ASR) to 4.35% under 20% pollution and 10% missing-source stress, versus 9.32% for the strongest runtime re-execution baseline. Under a matched 38.87% review budget, post-review ASR is 2.54% versus 5.19%. Unseen-template and LANL deterministic-profile replays preserve the advantage. In a 400-case LANL replay on each of two provider-returned LLMs, PACEGuard has no observed ASR or poisoned-citation events among 200 polluted cases per model (0/200; 95% one-sided exact upper bound 1.49%), with 0-0.75% review. Parameter and seed/temperature sweeps show the same observed zero-event outcome; these are finite-suite measurements, not evidence of zero deployment risk. title: From Mathematical Problems to the Generation of Problems: Generative Audit, Methodology, and an Open Worldview in GHT
summary: Generative History Theory (GHT) begins not by adding another property to already constituted mathematical objects, but by auditing how an object acquires the admissibility to count as an object at all. Bare occurrence is marked by the boundary notation A=0 but does not enter mathematics. Mathematics begins when an occurrence that has already ended leaves a re-addressable trace; subsequent directedness allows that trace to re-enter the present relation, through which distinction, re-identification, relation, composition, invariance, and scale acquire stable expression. The Generative History Law N → N+n further requires every new act of directedness, interpretation, proof, or retrospection to occur within an already accumulated history and to enter the background available for subsequent inquiry. On this foundation, the paper synthesizes the methodological and worldview consequences of the first two papers in the GHT Foundations of Mathematics Series. It elevates identity restoration into the more general framework of GHT generative audit. Generative audit contains two complementary movements: starting-point audit, which asks where the objects, identities, operational backgrounds, scales, and equivalence relations of a proposition acquired their admissibility; and generative abduction, which traces the genealogy of objectification backward from a mature proposition in order to determine whether a present difficulty reflects genuinely new mathematical structure, a real change of identity, a gap in cross-background transport, or proof debt generated by objectification itself. The paper develops the notions of identity recession, identity re-proof loops, over-splitting, over-merging, operation-type audit, provenance continuity, and the Preserved/Hidden/Destroyed (P/H/D) ledger. It also examines the multiplicative provenance of Prime and asks how proof obligations may arise when mature representations obscure their common generative history. The Riemann Hypothesis serves as the principal high-pressure example inherited from Paper II. Goldbach-type questions are retained explicitly as an open direction rather than presented as a completed proof. The Yang–Mills mass-gap problem and other difficult mathematical problems are likewise treated as exploratory interfaces for generative audit, not as automatic consequences of GHT. Finally, the paper extends generative audit toward a broader open worldview. Mathematics, physics, computation, life, cognition, language, the humanities, and social knowledge all depend in different ways on addressability, directedness, re-identification, objectification, and stable expression. GHT therefore proposes interfaces rather than annexation: whatever can become a stable object may be asked for its addressable provenance, relational history, mode of directedness, and cost of objectification. This is Paper III and the methodological synthesis of the initial GHT Foundations of Mathematics three-paper series.
